Administration of Medications

Medication administration — rights, routes, safety and the nurse's responsibilities.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • State the rights of medication administration
  • Describe common routes of drug administration
  • Explain medication safety and error prevention

In simple words

Medication administration is giving prescribed drugs safely and correctly. Errors can harm or even kill patients, so strict checking is essential.

The nurse checks the prescription, prepares the drug, gives it by the right route, observes the patient and documents everything.

Rights of medication administration

Right What to check
Right patient Name and ID band
Right drug Name matches prescription
Right dose Correct amount and calculation
Right route Oral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, etc.
Right time Correct time and frequency
Right reason Why the drug is given
Right documentation Record after giving

Common routes

Route Examples Notes
Oral Tablets, syrups Safest, most common
Intravenous (IV) Injection, infusion Fast action; monitor closely
Intramuscular (IM) Into muscle Vaccines, some antibiotics
Subcutaneous Under skin Insulin, heparin
Topical Creams, ointments Local effect

Medication safety

  • Check the label three times: when taking from storage, before pouring, before giving.
  • Do not leave medications unattended.
  • Calculate doses carefully; have another nurse check high-risk doses.
  • Report errors immediately — do not hide them.
  • Watch for allergic reactions and side effects.

🔴 Check three times

Check the medication label three times — when taking it from storage, before preparing and before giving. Never give a drug you have not checked yourself.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Before giving — check all rights; know the drug’s action, dose and side effects.
  • During administration — stay with the patient; ensure the drug is swallowed or given correctly.
  • After giving — observe for effect and adverse reactions; document immediately.
  • Errors — report immediately; follow hospital policy; do not blame or hide.
  • High-risk drugs — insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy — double-check with another nurse.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Rights: right patient, drug, dose, route, time, reason, documentation.
  2. Check the label three times before giving any medication.
  3. Routes: oral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, topical.
  4. Report medication errors immediately; do not hide them.
  5. Double-check high-risk drugs with another nurse.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Know the drug’s action, dose, side effects and contraindications before giving.
  2. Never leave medications unattended at the bedside.
  3. Calculate doses carefully; verify with another nurse when unsure.
  4. Document after giving, not before.

📌 Memory trick

Rights: “P-D-D-R-T-R-D” — Patient, Drug, Dose, Route, Time, Reason, Documentation.

60-second revision

  • Medication rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time, reason, documentation.
  • Check label three times.
  • Routes: oral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, topical.
  • Report errors immediately.
  • Double-check high-risk drugs.

Test yourself

Which is NOT a right of medication administration?

Answer: C. There is no 'right colour' — the rights are patient, drug, dose, route, time, reason and documentation.

The safest and most common route is:

Answer: C. Oral administration is the safest and most common route.

If a medication error occurs, the nurse should:

Answer: B. Report medication errors immediately so the patient can be monitored and protected.

High-risk drugs include:

Answer: B. Insulin, heparin, opioids and chemotherapy are high-risk and need double-checking.

Medication should be documented:

Answer: B. Document immediately after giving the medication.
